newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Black South African investors moving into new phase.
newsitem.headline: Black South African investors moving into new phase.

text.p: Black South African investment executives said on Wednesday their empowerment strategy was now seeking to build skills and employment through greater management involvement and greenfield operations.

Key black deal-makers Cyril Ramaphosa and Donald Ncube, visiting Australia for an investment conference, said black investment to date had been characterised by a low-risk strategy of buying units from white-controlled conglomerates.

"I think the second phase is going to be seen as businesses getting into or buying into...businesses where they can get close to the operations...moving more and more away from just being holding companies," Ramaphosa told reporters.
"That is not to say that you don't have black business that is already involved in the operations," the ex-union boss said.

Ramaphosa and Ncube spoke of the progress of black empowerment at a joint news conference on the final day of a three-day investment conference in Australia targeted primarily at increasing trade with Asia.

Ramaphosa, deputy chairman of South Africa's largest black-controlled business, New Africa Investments Ltd, pointed to last week's purchase of a controlling interest in mining house JCI Ltd by Capital Alliance Holdings Ltd as heartening evidence of a new phase in black empowerment.

"Mining has played such a crucial role in the development of the South African economy. I think it is pleasing for us as black people to know that we (are) beginning to arrive at the...height of the economy of our country," he said.

New and existing black businesses were braving start-up operations in sectors such as broadcasting, casinos, and lotteries, said Ncube, who is executive chairman of black industrial group Real Africa Holdings Ltd (RAH).
"That is where they have greater opportunity of creating jobs," Ramaphosa said.
Both men agreed that acquisitions in South Africa's finance sector by NAIL and RAH would continue to bolster opportunities for new black businesses.

NAIL has a 30 percent stake in life insurer Metropolitan Life, while RAH has interests in a number of financial service firms including an asset management joint venture with financial services giant Sanlam.

"We are able to leverage funds for (emerging black businesses), and a number of those black companies feel that they are so confident that they can go out on their own, in their own name and right to leverage funds," Ramaphosa said.
Ncube said it was crucial that investment intentions at corporate level be matched by the building of the black population's skills base, an education denied under the apartheid regime.
"The next challenge that is facing us is to now acquire those skills so we can get into areas of technology, so we can get into areas of adding value and increasing jobs," he said.
"This is the first step in a journey of one thousand miles. It is just the beginning and not the end," Ncube added.
